Well, thank you for fitting me in, doctor. I, uh... I guess the main thing that brings me in today is that I just keep messing up these little things. It’s, well, it’s getting really frustrating for me, to be honest. 

Like, for example, I spend a fair bit of time down at the senior center nowadays—just to get out of the house, you know, keep myself busy since I'm not working anymore—and I was helping them out with this class sheet the other day. All I had to do was write down the schedule. But I end up writing the completely wrong time on the sign-up sheet. So then you've got people showing up at the wrong hour, getting irritated, and it's a whole big confusion, all because I just didn't look closely enough at the paper when I was copying it down. 

And it happens with my hobbies out in the garage, too. I like to do a little woodwork, and, well, you know the old rule, 'measure twice, cut once.' I'll measure a board, look right at it, and I still end up cutting it a hair short. It’s like my eyes just completely skip over the small print or those tiny little fraction lines on the tape measure. And let me tell you, lumber is way too expensive right now to be throwing away perfectly good pieces of oak or pine just because I glossed over the details. It’s just... it's always these little errors, over and over, and it makes a guy feel foolish after a while.

Well, gosh, doctor, that’s... that’s a really good question, and to be perfectly honest with you, I’m not really sure I know the answer to it. I’ve sat there and chewed on that exact thing myself, wondering where exactly the train goes off the tracks. Because, you see, it’s not like I’m walking around all day with the wrong number in my head. At least, I don't think I am. 

Like with that sign-up sheet at the center—I was sitting right there at the folding table, and the master copy was maybe three inches from my left hand. I look at it, I see 'Tuesday at 2:00 PM.' I know it says two. But then I move my eyes over to the blank sheet, I uncap my pen—which, by the way, was one of those nice gel pens they keep at the front desk, so it wasn't like I was struggling to write or distracted by a dry ink cartridge—and my hand just puts down a three. Did I forget it in that half-second? Did my hand just do its own thing? I couldn't tell you. 

Same thing out in the garage with the wood. I'll see fourteen and three-quarters on the tape, walk two steps over to the miter saw, and suddenly I'm lining the blade up on the one-quarter mark. I don't know if I'm remembering it wrong in that short walk, or if my brain just kind of... blurs the numbers together when it's time to actually do the writing or the cutting. My wife, she always tells me I just need to slow down, but the thing of it is, I am going slow! I'm taking my time, trying to be careful, and the mistake still slips in there somehow. So, yeah, I really couldn't say for sure if it's the memory or the writing part that's broken. I just know the final result ends up wrong.

Boy, you’re really hitting the nail on the head with these questions, doc, but... I just can't rightly say. I really can't. I’ve tried to catch myself in the act, you know? Just to see which one it is, because I've wondered the exact same thing.

I’ve got my reading glasses on—I even went and got new bifocals a few months back, thinking maybe it was just my eyes going bad on me and causing the mistakes, but the optometrist said my prescription barely changed. So I’m looking right at the details, staring a hole through ’em, and I think I’m focused. I really do. 

But then, is it that I wasn't actually focusing on the right part of the number, or did I just forget it two seconds later? It’s like... it’s like trying to hold water in your bare hands. You cup your hands tight, you think you’re paying attention to keeping your fingers closed, but the water just slips right through before you even realize it’s leaking. So maybe it is the memory? But then again, my memory isn't totally shot—I can tell you the batting averages of the '68 Tigers, and I remember my errands around town just fine. 

It just evaporates, right in that split second between looking and doing. So I guess... well, I just don't know which one is the real culprit. It could be either one. It’s a real puzzle, it truly is. And it drives my wife absolutely up the wall when I try to explain it to her, because she just says, 'Well, pay better attention to the details then!' And I tell her, 'Martha, I am trying!' It just... it doesn't seem to make a lick of difference whether I stare at it for one second or ten. I just don't know.

Well, now, that’s another tough one to pin down. You’re really asking the hard questions today, doc. I mean, I suppose everything requires you to remember something for at least a little bit, right? Even just walking from the kitchen to the living room, you’ve got to remember why you got up in the first place. But as for whether these mistakes happen *more* often when I have to hold onto information for a short bit... I really couldn't say for sure. 

I’ve thought about it, I really have. Like, I’ll sit in my armchair—the brown leather recliner I’ve had since I retired from the plant, it’s got a little tear on the left armrest but it’s still the most comfortable chair in the house—and I’ll just sit there and run through my day. I’ll think, 'Okay, did I mess up the grocery list because I had to remember it from the fridge to the notepad?' But then, sometimes I make a mistake when I’m looking right at the thing! Like I said with the sign-up sheet, the master copy was right there, practically touching my elbow. I wasn't carrying that information across the room or anything. 

So, I don't know if it’s the short-term memory part that’s the real issue. Sometimes it feels like it is, like when I measure the wood and walk to the saw. But other times, it just happens right there on the spot, no carrying or holding onto the information required. It’s like my brain just decides to scramble the signal, whether I’m holding onto it for five seconds or five milliseconds. So, to answer your question, I really haven't noticed a clear pattern there. It’s just... it’s all just a big jumble of little errors, and I can't quite figure out the rhyme or reason to it, no matter how much I sit and stew on it.

It’s just... it's always these little errors, over and over, and it makes a guy feel foolish after a while.\n\nDoctor: Do you usually remember the correct information, like the schedule or measurements, but just write it down incorrectly?\n\nPatient: Well, gosh, doctor, that’s... that’s a really good question, and to be perfectly honest with you, I’m not really sure I know the answer to it. I’ve sat there and chewed on that exact thing myself, wondering where exactly the train goes off the tracks. Because, you see, it’s not like I’m walking around all day with the wrong number in my head. At least, I don't think I am. \n\nLike with that sign-up sheet at the center—I was sitting right there at the folding table, and the master copy was maybe three inches from my left hand. I look at it, I see 'Tuesday at 2:00 PM.' I know it says two. But then I move my eyes over to the blank sheet, I uncap my pen—which, by the way, was one of those nice gel pens they keep at the front desk, so it wasn't like I was struggling to write or distracted by a dry ink cartridge—and my hand just puts down a three. Did I forget it in that half-second? Did my hand just do its own thing? I couldn't tell you. \n\nSame thing out in the garage with the wood. I'll see fourteen and three-quarters on the tape, walk two steps over to the miter saw, and suddenly I'm lining the blade up on the one-quarter mark. I don't know if I'm remembering it wrong in that short walk, or if my brain just kind of... blurs the numbers together when it's time to actually do the writing or the cutting. My wife, she always tells me I just need to slow down, but the thing of it is, I am going slow! I'm taking my time, trying to be careful, and the mistake still slips in there somehow. So, yeah, I really couldn't say for sure if it's the memory or the writing part that's broken. I just know the final result ends up wrong.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your mistakes happen because you're not paying attention to the details or because you forget the information right after you see it?\n\nPatient: Boy, you’re really hitting the nail on the head with these questions, doc, but... It just... it doesn't seem to make a lick of difference whether I stare at it for one second or ten. Like, I’ll sit in my armchair—the brown leather recliner I’ve had since I retired from the plant, it’s got a little tear on the left armrest but it’s still the most comfortable chair in the house—and I’ll just sit there and run through my day. I’ll think, 'Okay, did I mess up the grocery list because I had to remember it from the fridge to the notepad?' But then, sometimes I make a mistake when I’m looking right at the thing! Like I said with the sign-up sheet, the master copy was right there, practically touching my elbow. I wasn't carrying that information across the room or anything. \n\nSo, I don't know if it’s the short-term memory part that’s the real issue. Sometimes it feels like it is, like when I measure the wood and walk to the saw. But other times, it just happens right there on the spot, no carrying or holding onto the information required. It’s like my brain just decides to scramble the signal, whether I’m holding onto it for five seconds or five milliseconds. So, to answer your question, I really haven't noticed a clear pattern there. Well, doc, that's... that's another one I'm just not entirely sure about. I mean, learning new things? I haven't really picked up anything brand new in a good long while. Since I retired from the plant, I mostly stick to what I know. I’ve got my woodworking in the garage—which, like I said, has its own little hiccups—and my routine is pretty much set in stone these days. But that wasn't really learning something new, just going on a different day. Well, doc, that’s... I mean, focus is a funny word, isn't it? It’s like when people say 'pay attention.' I hear that one a lot, especially from Martha. But hard to focus on what I'm doing? I don't really know if I'd call it hard, per se. It’s not like I sit down at my workbench in the garage—the one I built myself back in '85, solid oak, sturdy as a rock—and think, 'Boy, I just can't focus on this piece of wood today.' I don't feel a struggle, you know? 

When I'm out there, making a birdhouse or fixing a wobbly chair leg, I feel like I'm right there in the moment. I've got my tools laid out, the radio playing softly in the background—usually that classic rock station, 104.3, they play the good stuff from the seventies—and I'm just working away. I don't feel like my mind is wandering off to Timbuktu or anything like that. I feel like I'm focused on the sanding, or the gluing, or whatever it is. 

But then, of course, there are those mistakes we talked about. The wrong measurements, the mixed-up numbers. So, if I'm making those mistakes, does that mean I'm *not* focused? Or does it mean I *am* focused, but just on the wrong thing? Or maybe my focus is just fine, and it's something else entirely causing the hiccups. It’s hard to say if the focus itself is the problem, because when I’m doing a task, I don't feel this big wall stopping me from concentrating. I feel like I'm doing it just fine... right up until I realize I've cut the board an inch too short. 

So, do I find it hard to focus? I honestly couldn't tell you yes or no. I don't notice a feeling of difficulty, if that makes sense. It just feels like I'm going about my business normally, and then... oops, another little error slips in. So I'm just not sure if focus is the right word for it, doc. I really aren't.

Well, doc, mentally foggy... cloudy... see, that’s another one of those things where I just don't quite know how to answer you. I hear folks my age talk about that a lot, you know? Down at the senior center, they’ll say, 'Oh, my brain’s just in a fog today,' or 'I can't think straight, it’s all cloudy.' But when they say that, they usually mean they can't remember their grandchild's name, or they forgot where they parked the car at the grocery store. And like I said, my memory for that kind of stuff is usually pretty sharp. I know exactly where I parked—third row, next to the cart return, always try to get that spot so nobody dings my doors.

But as for this feeling of... of fog? I don't really think I feel that. When I’m sitting in my recliner, or out in the garage, I don't feel like there’s cotton stuffed in my head, or like I’m looking through a dirty windshield. My thoughts seem pretty clear to me. I think about what I want to do, and I go do it. If I want to build a birdhouse, I picture the birdhouse, I think about the wood I need, the nails, the paint... it all seems perfectly clear in my mind. There’s no haze over it. 

It’s just that somewhere between that clear thought and the actual doing of it, something goes a little wonky. Like the wires get crossed, but not because there’s a fog rolling in. It’s more like... well, I don't know what it’s like, to be honest. But it doesn't feel cloudy. I feel awake, I feel alert, I feel like I know exactly what’s going on around me. I can tell you what the weather is doing, what the neighbor’s dog is barking at, what Martha is cooking for dinner just by the smell—it's pot roast tonight, by the way, I can always tell when she uses that specific seasoning blend. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I feel foggy or cloudy. My brain feels like it’s running just fine, right up until I look down and realize I’ve written a 7 instead of a 4 on that sign-up sheet. And even then, I don't feel confused, I just feel... frustrated. Frustrated that I made a silly mistake when my head felt perfectly clear the whole time. So, I guess the short answer is no, I haven't really noticed any of that fogginess you're talking about. It just doesn't seem to fit what's going on with me.

Recipes... well, now, Martha does most of the day-to-day cooking around here, like that pot roast I mentioned. It’s the exact same thing out in the garage. If I buy a new piece of equipment, like the benchtop drill press I got last Christmas, it comes with a thick little booklet of instructions. So, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble following things with multiple steps. Whether it's chili or a drill press, I just take it one step at a time, and I get right to the finish line without any confusion.

Well, a sequence of actions... see, if it’s a recipe or an instruction manual like I was just saying, where somebody else has already figured out the exact steps for me, I’m perfectly fine. I just can't seem to line them up in my head: one, two, three. So if figuring out how to organize a day like that counts as a sequence of actions, then yes, I definitely get my wires crossed there.

It’s hard to say if the focus itself is the problem, because when I’m doing a task, I don't feel this big wall stopping me from concentrating. I feel like I'm doing it just fine... right up until I realize I've cut the board an inch too short. \n\nSo, do I find it hard to focus? I honestly couldn't tell you yes or no. I don't notice a feeling of difficulty, if that makes sense. It just feels like I'm going about my business normally, and then... oops, another little error slips in. So I'm just not sure if focus is the right word for it, doc. Numbers and diagrams? Oh, no, no, not at all. Actually, it's funny you bring that up, because that's probably one of the things I'm best at. You remember I was telling you about the woodworking, and prepping the materials for the Boy Scouts? Well, you really can't build a decent birdhouse, let alone a custom bookshelf or a coffee table, if you can't read a diagram. 

I've been subscribing to this magazine for years—Woodworker's Journal, it's a fantastic publication, comes in the mail every other month—and they always include these really intricate blueprints for their projects. They have these big, exploded views showing exactly how all the joints fit together, with all the specific measurements and angles printed right there on the page. I can look at one of those schematics, see all the fractions and the degrees for the miter cuts, and it all makes perfect sense to me instantly. I can just picture exactly how the flat drawing translates into a three-dimensional object in my hands. 

And it's the exact same story with numbers. I mean, I'm out in the garage reading the tiny little hash marks on a tape measure down to the sixteenth of an inch, doing the math in my head to figure out where to make the cut. "Measure twice, cut once," just like my old shop teacher Mr. Henderson used to drill into our heads back in high school. I never get the numbers jumbled up. 

It's actually kind of ironic, when you think about it. You can hand me a highly detailed, complicated schematic for a grandfather clock with a hundred different pieces, and I can read it and understand exactly how it all fits together without breaking a sweat. But you ask me to figure out whether I should go to the hardware store before or after the post office on a Tuesday afternoon, and my brain just completely shorts out. So, no, reading things on paper, looking at pictures or numbers or charts... I've never had a lick of trouble with any of that.

Oh, boy. Now that... see, that right there is the nail on the head. That’s exactly what I’ve been trying to get at when I was talking about my daily schedule earlier. Deciding what to do first? It’s... well, it’s a real problem for me. 

Take a typical busy day, for instance. Let’s say I’ve got a few errands to run out in town—maybe I need to pick up some more of that wood glue from the hardware store and drop off a package at the post office for Martha. And on top of that, I’ve got a workshop to get ready for, you know, getting all the materials prepped and sorted out for the Boy Scouts like I mentioned before. And then, to top it all off, I’ve got an appointment on the exact same day, maybe a dentist appointment or something right in the middle of the afternoon. 

Now, you'd think a grown man could just look at that list and say, "Okay, one, two, three, let's go." But I look at those tasks and I just... I completely freeze up. I have the hardest time trying to put them in any kind of logical order. I'll sit there at the kitchen table, drinking my morning coffee, and my brain just spins and spins. I'll think, should I go to the hardware store first, then the post office, then come back and do the wood, then go to the doctor? Or should I do the workshop prep first so my hands are clean for the dentist? 

So what usually happens is... well, I end up just kind of starting one thing, like I'll go out to the garage and start pulling out the lumber for the workshop. But then, five minutes in, I'll think, "Oh, wait, the post office line is going to get long if I don't go right now," so I stop what I'm doing, leave the boards half-stacked on the workbench, and go inside to grab my car keys. But then I walk inside and realize I haven't even changed my clothes for the appointment yet. So I stop again.

It's really just the organizing and the planning part that gets me all tangled up, like I was explaining before with the daily schedule, but just holding onto a quick list of things or a number? No, my brain is pretty much a steel trap for that kind of stuff.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble reading or understanding visual information, such as numbers or diagrams?\n\nPatient: Numbers and diagrams? You remember I was telling you about the woodworking, and prepping the materials for the Boy Scouts? They have these big, exploded views showing exactly how all the joints fit together, with all the specific measurements and angles printed right there on the page. I can look at one of those schematics, see all the fractions and the degrees for the miter cuts, and it all makes perfect sense to me instantly. I can just picture exactly how the flat drawing translates into a three-dimensional object in my hands. \n\nAnd it's the exact same story with numbers. I mean, I'm out in the garage reading the tiny little hash marks on a tape measure down to the sixteenth of an inch, doing the math in my head to figure out where to make the cut. \"Measure twice, cut once,\" just like my old shop teacher Mr. Henderson used to drill into our heads back in high school. I never get the numbers jumbled up. \n\nIt's actually kind of ironic, when you think about it. You can hand me a highly detailed, complicated schematic for a grandfather clock with a hundred different pieces, and I can read it and understand exactly how it all fits together without breaking a sweat. Now, Susan has this awkward little alcove in her living room, right next to her brick fireplace, and you can't just buy a piece of furniture from a big box store to fit in there. Step two is heading down to the lumber yard—and you have to pick a good hardwood, like oak or maybe a nice cherry, because you don't want to use pine for a bookshelf. Pine is too soft, it’ll just bow under the weight of all those heavy hardcovers. Anyway, step three is ripping the boards down on the table saw. Then you’ve got your routing, your sanding—and you can't rush the sanding, you gotta start with an 80 grit, move up to a 120, and finish off with a 220 so it’s smooth as glass before you even think about applying the stain. Just until you can smell 'em, maybe thirty seconds a side. Any longer and they get bitter. Then you soak them in hot beef broth for exactly twenty minutes before you blend them up into a paste. After that, it’s searing the meat in small batches so it browns instead of steams, sweating the onions, blooming the spices... well, you get the picture. It’s a whole big process that takes the better part of an afternoon. \n\nAnd I follow that recipe right down to the letter every single time. I keep the paper printed out on the counter, and I just go right down the list. I don’t get lost or skip a step. \n\nIt’s the exact same thing out in the garage. If I buy a new piece of equipment, like the benchtop drill press I got last Christmas, it comes with a thick little booklet of instructions. I just empty the box, lay out all the parts on my workbench—the bolts, the washers, the brackets, grouping them all by size—and I go step one, step two, step three, right through to the end. It all makes perfect sense to me as long as the manufacturer actually wrote it down clearly and didn't just give you a bunch of blurry pictures. \n\nSo, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble following things with multiple steps. Whether it's chili or a drill press, I just take it one step at a time, and I get right to the finish line without any confusion.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble remembering a sequence of actions you need to perform in a specific order?\n\nPatient: Well, a sequence of actions... see, if it’s a recipe or an instruction manual like I was just saying, where somebody else has already figured out the exact steps for me, I’m perfectly fine. I like to pre-cut the pieces so the kids don't have to use the heavy power saws, which means I need a good hour or two out in the garage.
